title: 情報戦に負けた戦後日本　高市首相、インテリジェンス強化への条件
extracted_text:
高市早苗政権はインテリジェンス（情報収集・分析）能力を高めることを目指し、「スパイ防止法」の制定を視野に入れる。戦後の日本が外国からの政治工作に無防備だったことを受けた改革といえる。その原因は組織や法律がなかったからなのだろうか。

ドイツ連邦公文書館に毛筆でしたためた一通の手紙が眠る。「友好の輪をより大きくするためにも閣下が一日も早くわが国を訪問されますことを望む次第です」。差出人は自民党の佐藤一郎衆院議員。大蔵官僚出身で経済企画庁長官などの要職を務めた政治家だ。

1984年6月、事務所の封筒に入れ、共産圏の中核国家だった東独の国家指導層のミッターク政治局員に送った。

3カ月後、重ねて書簡を送る。「閣下の訪日は必ずや両国の相互友好発展に多大な貢献をなすものと確信」と誘った。外務省も東独政府に「いまが好機」と伝え、訪日を促した。

日本が東独との通商拡大に前のめりだ――。そう判断したミッターク氏はすぐには動かず、少しじらして86年に東独の政府専用機で堂々と日本に降り立つ。

表向きは友好親善を装ったが、随行員には腹心の謀略家、シャルク・ゴロトコフスキ貿易次官を選んだ。ソ連国家保安委員会（KGB）に直結する情報機関、国家保安省の大佐で、産業スパイの統括役である。

スパイを自ら呼び込んでしまった日本。結末は明らかだった。東独は経済官僚や大使館員を総動員し、ハイテク企業に接触した。東芝などが東独の半導体量産に協力することを決めた。

ミッターク氏は帰国後、報告書に誇らしげに書き込んだ。「交渉の結果、何社かの日本企業は禁輸品を渡すことに同意した」。独裁国家の真の姿を直視せず、交流に取り組む政治家を利用した。

東独と関係をもったのは佐藤氏だけではない。檜垣徳太郎、鍋島直紹、河野謙三、桜内義雄の各氏。東独の機密文書には自民党議員が多く登場する。なかには結果的に対日工作の便宜につながったような記録もある。商談を仲介するような例もみられた。

日本政府も認識が甘かった。「日本の半導体製造装置が東南アジア経由で東独に流れている」。米国は水面下で日本に警告した。外務省は「不審な点はない」と素通りしていた。

なぜ「スパイ天国」を許してしまったのか。自民党も政府も財界も危機感がなかったのが最大の問題ではないか。日本は「不都合な事実」や「負の過去」を直視するのが苦手だ。

いまも日本はロシアでの資源ビジネスにこだわる。デュアルユース（軍民両用）の日本製品は東南アジアなどを通じてロシアに流れている。サプライチェーン（供給網）には中国が深く組み込まれている。それを注視する欧米の情報機関を取材すると、冷戦時代と変わらぬ日本の「危機感の欠如」や「事なかれ主義」を憂える声が聞こえる。

日本が再び情報戦で負けないようにインテリジェンス機能は高めた方がいい。それは政府・与党を守るのではなく民主主義を守るツールでなくてはならない。

東京大学の井形彬特任講師はインテリジェンス改革を「緊急課題」としつつ、独立した第三者機関や裁判所による承認などで乱用を防ぐ仕組みが大切だとクギを刺す。不服申立制度なども必要だという。

将来の開示を前提に活動記録を文書で残すことや国会による民主的統制も考慮すべきだろう。なにより国民に丁寧に説明し、社会全体で危機感を共有することが不可欠だ。それが高市政権の優先課題ではないか。

（欧州駐在編集委員　赤川省吾）

translated_text:
The Sanae Takaichi administration aims to enhance intelligence (information gathering and analysis) capabilities, and is considering enacting an "anti-espionage law." This can be seen as a reform in response to Japan's defenselessness against foreign political operations in the postwar era. Was the cause simply that there were no organizations or laws in place?

A letter written inbrush script lies dormant in the German Federal Archives. "We sincerely hope that Your Excellency will visit our country at the earliest possible opportunity to further expand the circle of friendship." The sender was Ichiro Sato, a member of the House of Representatives from the Liberal Democratic Party. He was a former Treasury bureaucrat who held key positions such as Director of the Economic Planning Agency.

In June 1984, he sent it in an office envelope to Mitwerk, a Politburo member of the East German leadership, which was a core communist nation.

Three months later, he sent another letter. "I am confident that Your Excellency's visit will surely make a tremendous contribution to the development of mutual friendship between our two countries," he invited. The Foreign Ministry also told the East German government that "now is the opportune time" and urged the visit.

Japan was eager to expand trade with East Germany. Judging thus, Mitwerk did not act immediately but waited slightly, arriving in Japan in 1986 on an official East German government plane.

On the surface, they pretended friendship, but among his accompanying staff he chose his trusted strategist, Trade Deputy Director Schalk Gorotokov. He was a colonel of the state security apparatus directly connected to the Soviet KGB, the State Security Ministry, and served as the coordinator of industrial espionage.

Japan had invited spies on its own. The outcome was clear. East Germany mobilized economic bureaucrats and embassy staff en masse and approached high-tech companies. Toshiba and others decided to cooperate with East Germany's semiconductor mass production.

Mitwerk proudly wrote in his report after returning to Japan. "As a result of negotiations, several Japanese companies agreed to provide contraband items." They utilized politicians who did not face the true nature of the authoritarian state and engaged in exchange.

Sato was not the only one who had relations with East Germany. Each of Tokutaro Higaki, Naotsugu Nabeshima, Kenzo Konno, and Yoshio Sakurauch. Many LDP lawmakers appear in East German classified documents. Among them are records that ultimately facilitated anti-Japanese operations. There are also examples of mediating business transactions.

The Japanese government was also naive in its awareness. "Japanese semiconductor manufacturing equipment is flowing to East Germany via Southeast Asia." The US warned Japan covertly. The Foreign Ministry brushed it off, saying there were "no suspicious points."

Why was the "espionage paradise" allowed to happen? The biggest problem may be that neither the LDP, the government, nor the business circle had a sense of crisis. Japan is poor at facing "inconvenient facts" or a "negative past."

Japan is still obsessed with resource business in Russia. Japanese dual-use (civilian and military) products are flowing to Russia via Southeast Asia and elsewhere. China is deeply integrated into the supply chain. When interviewed, Western intelligence agencies that monitor this express concern about Japan's "lack of crisis awareness" and "non-interventionist attitude" remaining unchanged from the Cold War era.

It would be better to strengthen intelligence functions so Japan does not lose in the intelligence war again. This must be a tool to protect democracy, not just the government and ruling party.

Tokyo University specially appointed lecturer Akira Ikeda, while calling intelligence reform an "urgent issue," emphasizes the importance of mechanisms to prevent abuse through approval by independent third-party institutions or courts. An appeal system is also necessary.

It should also be considered to keep activity records in documents on the premise of future disclosure and to have democratic control by the Diet. Most importantly, it is essential to explain carefully to citizens and share a sense of crisis throughout society. Is that not the priority of the Takaichi administration?

(European Bureau Chief Editorengo Akagawa)
title_en: Postwar Japan Lost in the Intelligence War: Prime Minister Takaichi Outlines Conditions for Strengthening Intelligence
